Selling During a Separation
Introduction

Selling the house during a separation or divorce adds an emotional and legal layer to an already demanding transaction. With a clear framework and the right professionals, you can get through it fairly and calmly.
This guide maps out the key points: the property's legal status depending on your situation, the decisions to make together, splitting the sale proceeds, and the role of a neutral broker.
Informational content, not legal advice: rely on a notary or a lawyer. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

Selling during a separation adds an emotional load to an already demanding process. This guide helps you stay on course: understanding the property's status, choosing between selling, buying out or waiting, setting the price together, splitting the proceeds and staying functional despite the conflict.
The through-line: structure and delegate so that emotion doesn't cost money.
Understanding the property's status
Knowing who owns what depending on your situation.
Knowing who owns what depending on your situation.

Your rights to the property depend on your situation: married (with the family patrimony rules), in a civil union, or common-law partners (whose rights differ depending on whether they are co-owners on title or not). This is a crucial and often misunderstood point.
Married / in a civil union: the family residence is governed by specific rules.
Common-law partners: rights largely depend on who is listed on title.
A legal opinion clarifies your exact situation.

Your rights to the property depend on your status: married/in a civil union (family patrimony), or common-law (the written agreement and the title prevail). Clarifying who owns what is the first step — it drives the split and the decisions to come.
Emilie's tip
Never assume your rights to the house without a legal opinion, especially in a common-law union. Clarifying the status from the start avoids painful conflicts and blockages later.
Deciding: sell, buy out or wait
Choosing the option that suits both parties.
Choosing the option that suits both parties.
Sell and split the proceeds: often the cleanest solution.
One buys out the other's share: possible if the buyout is financeable (borrowing capacity, net equity).
Wait (e.g. until a specific moment): sometimes chosen, but to be framed by a written agreement.
Each option has financial, tax and practical implications. A clear decision, put in writing, avoids misunderstandings.

Three options: sell and split (often the most neutral), one partner buys out the other's share, or wait (rarely ideal). The right choice depends on your means, the feasibility of the buyout and your need to turn the page. Decide together, in writing if possible.
Emilie's tip
Decide on the option and put it in writing, ideally with your advisors. A clear agreement on “who does what and when” hugely reduces the tensions of the process.
Setting the price and managing the sale together
Selling effectively despite the context.
Selling effectively despite the context.
Like any sale, you start from a comparative analysis to set a fair price. The difficulty is more human: two people have to agree on the price, the visits, and which offers to accept.
Rely on neutral facts (CMA) to depersonalize the price.
Define in advance how decisions (offers) will be made.
Keep the property presentable despite the context.

Like any sale, you start from a comparative analysis to set a fair price and you prepare the property. The difficulty is coordinating as two in a tense context: entrust the logistics and communication to a neutral broker so that each decision doesn't become a confrontation.
Emilie's tip
Entrust the sale to a neutral broker who speaks to both parties as equals. A professional intermediary reduces friction and keeps the transaction on the rails.
Splitting the sale proceeds
Clarifying the split and the financial aspects.
Clarifying the split and the financial aspects.

The split of the net proceeds (after repaying the mortgage and the fees) depends on your legal situation and your agreements. The notary can handle the distribution at closing according to the agreed instructions.
Also anticipate your needs for what comes next: each of you will probably have to find new housing. Understanding your post-sale purchasing or renting capacity is part of an informed decision.

The split of the net proceeds (after repaying the mortgage and the fees) depends on your status and your agreements. Clarify it in advance and, if needed, have it legally framed: an unclear split is a major source of last-minute conflicts.
Emilie's tip
Have it specified in writing, before closing, how the net proceeds will be split. The notary will follow those instructions; improvising it on signing day is a guaranteed source of conflict.

Staying functional despite the conflict protects your money: agree on the key decisions in advance, go through neutral intermediaries and separate the financial issues from personal tensions. A broker as the single channel of communication defuses a lot of tension.
Emilie's tip
Entrusting the sale to a neutral broker avoids many direct confrontations. They become the single channel of communication about the transaction, which protects the sale — and often your energy.

Resources & glossary
Family patrimony: rules governing the residence of married/civil-union couples.
Common-law partners: rights largely depending on registration on title.
Net proceeds: the amount after repaying the mortgage and the fees.
Share buyout: an option where one partner buys out the other's share.
Neutral broker: an intermediary who facilitates the sale between the parties.
Family patrimony: protections for married/civil-union couples.
Common-law partners: no automatic protections; the title and the written agreement prevail.
Share buyout: one partner buys the other's share to keep the property.
Net proceeds: the sum remaining after mortgage and fees, to be split.
Mediation: neutral support to facilitate decisions.
